title: Reverse Exchange Coordination
name: Reverse Exchange Coordination
metaTitle: Reverse Exchange Coordination in Dallas, TX
metaDescription: Reverse 1031 exchange coordination for Dallas buyers: parking the replacement property, EAT structuring, and matching sale timing to the deadlines.

sections.html:
A reverse exchange comes up constantly in a market like Dallas, where the right building sometimes appears before an investor has even listed their relinquished property. The mechanics are more involved than a standard forward exchange, since title to one property has to be parked with a separate entity while the other side of the deal catches up, and the deadlines run just as hard as they do in a normal exchange.

Investors sometimes hear the word reverse and assume it means more flexibility, when in practice it usually means more coordination up front, since the financing and legal structure both need to be settled before anyone signs a contract on the replacement property.

sections.heading: Why an Investor Ends Up Doing It in Reverse
sections.html:
Reverse structures show up most often when a Dallas replacement property, particularly a net-lease or industrial building with limited competing inventory, needs to move faster than an investor's existing property can be marketed and sold. Rather than lose the deal, the investor parks the new property first and sells the old one on a more normal timeline afterward.

It also comes up when a relinquished property has a complicated ownership structure, multiple family members or partners who need time to agree on listing terms, while the replacement opportunity in front of them won't wait that long for a decision.

sections.heading: How the Exchange Accommodation Titleholder Fits In
sections.html:
Under the safe harbor structure most practitioners rely on, an exchange accommodation titleholder, a separate entity unrelated to the investor, takes and holds title to either the replacement or the relinquished property for the duration of the parking arrangement. That entity typically works alongside your qualified intermediary, and the two roles need to be coordinated from the outset rather than treated as separate transactions.

Setting up the accommodation titleholder entity takes real lead time, usually a matter of weeks rather than days, which is one more reason a reverse structure needs to be identified as the likely path as early in the process as possible.

sections.heading: The Deadlines Still Apply, Just Mirrored
sections.html: A reverse exchange still runs on a 45-day identification period and a 180-day completion window, they just point in the other direction. The investor has 45 days to identify which property will be treated as relinquished if there's more than one candidate, and 180 days total to complete the sale of the relinquished property and unwind the parking arrangement.

sections.heading: What We Coordinate Once a Parking Arrangement Starts
sections.html:
Once a reverse structure is underway, we track a specific set of moving pieces:

  • Qualified exchange accommodation agreement execution date, which starts both clocks
  • Marketing and pricing plan for the relinquished Dallas property, set before or immediately after parking begins
  • Financing on the parked property, since most reverse deals require the investor to fund the purchase rather than use exchange proceeds that don't exist yet
  • Coordination between the EAT, the qualified intermediary, and both title companies on final unwind paperwork

sections.heading: Why Reverse Deals Need More Lead Time, Not Less
sections.html:
Because a reverse exchange requires financing arrangements and an accommodation titleholder that a standard forward exchange doesn't, we push for more lead time before a Dallas parking arrangement begins, not less. Investors sometimes assume a reverse structure buys them flexibility, but the 180-day total window is the same regardless of which direction the exchange runs.

A rushed reverse exchange, put together in the final days before a contract deadline, carries real risk of the accommodation agreement not being properly in place before title actually transfers, which can unravel the entire safe harbor structure after the fact.

faqs.q: When does a reverse exchange make sense for a Dallas investor?
faqs.a: It's most common when a strong replacement property, especially something with limited competing supply like a net-lease or industrial building, needs to close before the investor has sold their existing property. Parking the new property preserves the exchange rather than losing the deal outright to a competing buyer.

faqs.q: What is an exchange accommodation titleholder?
faqs.a: It's a separate entity, unrelated to the investor, that holds title to either the relinquished or replacement property during the parking period under the safe harbor structure most reverse exchanges use. It works alongside, not instead of, your qualified intermediary, and setting it up correctly takes real lead time before closing on the parked property.

faqs.q: Does the 180-day deadline change in a reverse exchange?
faqs.a: No. The total window is still 180 days from when the parking arrangement begins, and the investor still has 45 days within that to identify which property will be treated as relinquished if more than one is being considered at the time.

faqs.q: Can exchange proceeds fund the initial purchase in a reverse structure?
faqs.a: Generally not, since there's no completed sale yet to generate exchange funds. Most reverse purchases require the investor to arrange financing or use their own capital to acquire the parked property up front, which is worth confirming with a lender before committing to the structure.

faqs.q: How much lead time should a Dallas investor plan for before starting a reverse exchange?
faqs.a: More than a standard forward exchange, not less, because financing and the accommodation agreement both need to be in place before the parking period starts. We push for that lead time up front rather than treating it as something to sort out after the clock is already running, since retrofitting the structure mid-transaction rarely goes smoothly.
